name: Substitution Reactions
what: Substitution reactions involve replacing one atom or group of atoms in a molecule with another. This section covers two main types: halogenation of alkanes under UV light, and reactions of haloalkanes with hydroxide ions or ammonia.
why: Substitution reactions are a foundational tool in organic synthesis, allowing chemists to introduce new functional groups such as halogens, hydroxyl groups and amino groups into carbon chains. Understanding these reactions is essential for designing multi-step synthesis pathways.

items.title: I can classify a reaction as a substitution reaction given an equation or description
items.what: A substitution reaction is one where an atom or group of atoms in a molecule is replaced by a different atom or group of atoms, leaving the carbon skeleton intact.
items.why: Correctly identifying reaction type is the first step in predicting products and writing equations. Misclassifying a reaction leads to incorrect products and lost marks.
items.example: In the reaction CH3CH2Br + NaOH(aq) → CH3CH2OH + NaBr, the Br is replaced by OH, making this a substitution reaction.

items.title: I can write the equation for the halogenation of an alkane under UV light to form a haloalkane
items.what: Alkanes react with Cl2 or Br2 in the presence of UV light. A halogen atom replaces one hydrogen atom on the alkane, producing a haloalkane and a hydrogen halide (HCl or HBr) as a by-product.
items.why: This is one of the primary methods to introduce a halogen functional group onto a saturated carbon chain, which can then be used as an intermediate in further synthesis steps.
items.example: CH3CH3 + Br2 → CH3CH2Br + HBr (UV light). Ethane reacts with bromine under UV light to give bromoethane and hydrogen bromide.

items.title: I can explain why halogenation of larger alkanes can produce a mixture of positional isomers
items.what: When an alkane has more than one type of hydrogen (e.g. on different carbons), the halogen can substitute at any of those positions, leading to a mixture of structurally different haloalkane products.
items.why: Understanding this limitation is important when designing efficient synthesis pathways. A mixture of products reduces the yield of the desired compound and complicates purification.
items.example: Propane reacting with Cl2 under UV light gives both 1-chloropropane (Cl on carbon 1) and 2-chloropropane (Cl on carbon 2) simultaneously.

items.title: I can write the equation for the reaction of a haloalkane with aqueous NaOH or KOH to form a primary alcohol
items.what: Haloalkanes react with aqueous metal hydroxides such as NaOH(aq) or KOH(aq). The hydroxide ion (OH−) replaces the halogen atom, producing an alcohol and a metal halide salt as a by-product.
items.why: This reaction is a key step in multi-step pathways for synthesising primary alcohols and ultimately carboxylic acids from alkane or alkene starting materials.
items.example: CH3CH2CH2Cl + NaOH(aq) → CH3CH2CH2OH + NaCl. 1-chloropropane reacts with aqueous sodium hydroxide to give propan-1-ol and sodium chloride.

items.title: I can write the equation for the reaction of a haloalkane with ammonia to form a primary amine
items.what: Haloalkanes react with ammonia (NH3). The NH2 group from ammonia replaces the halogen atom, installing an amino group on the carbon chain. The by-product is a hydrogen halide such as HCl, HBr or HI.
items.why: This substitution reaction is one of only two pathways in the study design for synthesising primary amines, making it an essential reaction to know for multi-step synthesis questions.
items.example: CH3CH2Br + NH3 → CH3CH2NH2 + HBr. Bromoethane reacts with ammonia to give ethanamine and hydrogen bromide.
